rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. Their elution window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity tests.
The first method already achieves the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 1 as the optimal-score fallback.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the speed limit for full resolution; the critical pair is now close to the R = 1.5 threshold. Injection 2 remains a faster maximum-CRF fallback if this step compresses that pair too much.

Test whether higher temperature shifts the critical pair's selectivity enough to recover full resolution at the shorter gradient. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect, while injection 2 preserves the maximum-score fallback.

Return to the fully resolving 8-minute gradient and test a moderate temperature increase to shorten retention. At 60 C several pairs became critical, so 50 C tests a compromise between speed and selectivity.

Shift the starting composition upward and trim the upper window while keeping the slope close to injection 5's fully resolving gradient. This should reduce retention times without the strong compression seen with the previous 6-minute gradients.

Raise the gradient window by one grid step while preserving slope and temperature to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. Monitor the first pair for compression as its retention approaches the solvent front; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a much steeper gradient to see whether the critical middle pair crosses elution order and separates again, potentially enabling a substantially faster method. Injection 7 already secures the maximum CRF, so this is an exploratory speed test.

Test lower temperature at the same steep gradient to shift the critical middle pair's selectivity, which may now have reversed elution order. This isolates the temperature response while retaining injection 7 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to the successful moderate-slope regime, raising the starting fraction to shorten retention while slightly reducing the slope to protect the critical middle pair. This tests whether a narrower gradient window can retain full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient.

Reduce the gradient slope one grid step to recover resolution of the middle pair while preserving the early-pair separation. This may achieve full resolution near injection 7's retention time with a shorter programmed gradient.

Explore a higher starting fraction with a steep gradient to test whether the middle pair separates on the reversed-order side of its selectivity crossover. The lower temperature may preserve early-pair retention; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Use an intermediate slope between injections 10 and 11 to refine the full-resolution speed boundary. The critical pair may remain near R = 1.5 while the last peak elutes slightly earlier than in injection 11.

Lower temperature by one step with injection 13's gradient to measure local selectivity changes near the full-resolution boundary. This should strengthen the early pair and show whether the critical middle pair can also recover the small resolution deficit.

Test a four-minute gradient with a lower starting fraction than injection 11 to strengthen both limiting pairs. The slightly steeper slope should offset some added retention, targeting a compact maximum-CRF method with more resolution margin.

Test whether a modest temperature increase can preserve middle-pair resolution with a slightly steeper four-minute gradient, shortening retention. The early pair is the main risk at 55 C; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Test a higher starting fraction with a substantially shallower gradient to compensate for middle-pair compression. Lowering temperature to 45 C should help retain separation of the early pair; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Lower injection 16's temperature one step to recover early-pair resolution while checking whether the middle pair remains above R = 1.5. This directly tests the faster four-minute gradient against the successful but slightly shallower injection 15.

The faster neighboring methods repeatedly leave the middle pair just below baseline resolution. Reduce injection 11's slope one step to establish a maximum-score method with a larger resolution margin while keeping retention comfortably below 10 minutes.

Lower the starting fraction and soften the slope relative to injection 16 to recover its early-pair resolution at 55 C. This tests a higher-temperature, fully resolved alternative while preserving injection 11 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 19's slope through the critical middle pair, then hold at 0.40 to test a two-minute programmed gradient. The last peaks will likely elute later during the hold, but this may retain maximum CRF with a shorter gradient and lower final organic fraction.

Test one temperature step below injection 15 to strengthen the early pair while retaining the middle pair's resolution margin. This targets another maximum-CRF method near the successful short-gradient region; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower injection 19's temperature one step to improve its limiting early-pair resolution while using the shallower slope to protect the middle pair. This targets a better-balanced maximum-CRF alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Steepen injection 23's gradient one step to shorten retention while testing whether its middle-pair resolution margin is sufficient. This also checks the fastest confirmed method's selectivity at a temperature 5 C lower, where the early pair is better separated.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower version of injection 15, targeting greater resolution margin for both limiting pairs while remaining comfortably below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 11 the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
